A thin conducting spherical shell is used as a concave spherical mirror. A point object placed on its principal axis at a distance $u=30\,\text{cm}$ from the pole forms a real image on the same axis at a distance $v=45\,\text{cm}$ from the pole. (Use the mirror formula with magnitudes: $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{1}{u}+\frac{1}{v}$.)

The same shell now serves as the **outer conductor** of a concentric spherical capacitor. A second thin conducting spherical shell is placed concentrically inside it such that the radial separation between the shells is $d=1.0\,\text{mm}$. The inner shell is grounded, and the outer shell is raised to potential $V=5.0\,\text{kV}$. Neglect edge effects and take $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times 10^{-12}\,\text{F/m}$.
